entry.title: Inside Gin’s Request Path: Context Pooling, the Radix Tree, and the abortIndex Trick

link.title: Inside Gin’s Request Path: Context Pooling, the Radix Tree, and the abortIndex Trick

entry.content:
Every Go developer has recited the claim: Gin is fast, up to forty times faster than the frameworks it replaced, with a “zero allocation router” — that is literally how the README advertises it. But when your p99 spikes or a middleware behaves oddly, the benchmark line does not help you. What actually happens between net/http handing over a request and your handler receiving a *gin.Context? Most of us ship services on this framework without ever having looked.

The confusion shows up in specific, everyday bugs. A middleware calls c.Abort() and yet the handler still finishes writing its response — why? You register a group middleware and a route handler and wonder whether the middleware runs once per group or once per request. You call ShouldBind on a GET endpoint with a JSON body and get form binding instead. You write validate:"required" tags and nothing validates. All four behaviors are deliberate, and all four are visible in a handful of files at the root of the repository.

This post is a source tour of gin-gonic/gin on the master branch, at the version the tree advertises as v1.12.0. Every symbol and every line number cited below was verified against the actual clone — gin.go, tree.go, context.go, routergroup.go, and the binding package — so what you read here is the code as it exists, not folklore. The two diagrams were generated from that same tree: first the big picture, then the detailed request path.

Overview of a Gin request: the pooled Context enters ServeHTTP, the per-method radix tree resolves handlers, the merged middleware chain runs, and binding with validation happens inside the final handler.

Reading the overview from left to right:

  • One Context per request, recycled: Engine.ServeHTTP pulls a *Context out of a sync.Pool, resets it, dispatches, and puts it back — the object never hits the heap per request. See Engine.ServeHTTP, L691.
  • Routing is dispatch over method-keyed trees: handleHTTPRequest scans Engine.trees for the tree matching c.Request.Method, so path lookup never touches routes for other verbs. See Engine.handleHTTPRequest, L719.
  • The lookup itself is a loop, not recursion: node.getValue walks byte-by-byte against a compressed indices string, which is where the “zero allocation” claim is earned. See node.getValue, L418.
  • Middleware is baked in at registration time: RouterGroup.combineHandlers copies group middleware plus your handler into one flat HandlersChain that is stored on the tree node — there is no per-request middleware resolution. See RouterGroup.combineHandlers, L277.
  • Flow control is a single int8 index: Context.Next advances c.index and invokes pending handlers; nothing more. See Context.Next, L197.
  • Abort is just an integer write: Context.Abort pins the index at abortIndex (math.MaxInt8 >> 1), which is why the current handler still runs to completion. See Context.Abort, L216.
  • Binding selects an engine from method plus Content-Type: binding.Default maps every GET to form binding and switches on MIME for bodies. See binding.Default, L95.
  • Validation happens after decode, not inside it: decodeJSON finishes unmarshalling and then calls validate, which delegates to go-playground/validator with the tag name binding. See defaultValidator.lazyinit, L93.

The detailed path: allocation-free Context reuse, the radix insert and lookup mechanics, the index-based middleware loop, the binding and validation handoff, and the 404, 405, trailing-slash and panic fallbacks.

ServeHTTP: One Context per Request, Never Two

Engine implements http.Handler, and its ServeHTTP is eleven lines that define the whole performance story. On the very first request, a sync.Once guard (routeTreesUpdated) rewrites escaped colons in the trees; after that it is free. Then pool.Get() retrieves a *Context, c.writermem.reset(w) re-points the embedded response writer at the fresh http.ResponseWriter, c.reset() clears state, and handleHTTPRequest(c) does the routing. When the chain returns, the Context goes straight back into the pool with pool.Put(c) — all visible at Engine.ServeHTTP, L691.

The pool constructor explains the reuse budget: allocateContext preallocates the Params slice to engine.maxParams and the skipped-node stack to engine.maxSections, both of which addRoute grows as you register wildcard routes (Engine.allocateContext, L266). Context.reset then re-uses those same backing arrays: it truncates Params and Errors to length zero, nils the query and form caches, and resets index to -1 (Context.reset, L103). Steady-state serving allocates nothing for the Context itself.

The Radix Tree: Where the Zero-Allocation Claim Comes From

Each HTTP method gets its own compressed radix tree. Engine.addRoute finds or creates the root per method and delegates to node.addRoute (Engine.addRoute, L387). Insertion splits edges on the longest common prefix, merges wildcard segments, and panics loudly on conflicting wildcards or duplicate paths (node.addRoute, L135). Children are re-sorted by hit priority as routes are added, so the hottest first byte is tested first (node.incrementChildPrio, L111).

Lookup is the payoff. getValue runs an explicit walk loop: it strips the current node’s prefix, compares the next path byte against the node’s indices string, and descends (node.getValue, L418). Wildcard children sit at the end of the child array; when the walk takes a wildcard detour it records a skippedNode frame first, so a static route can still win later via backtracking (skippedNode, L407). The returned nodeValue carries handlers, parameters, the full path, and a tsr flag (trailing-slash redirect recommendation) — three small structs, no maps, no closures (nodeValue, L400).

Back in handleHTTPRequest, a match assigns c.handlers and c.fullPath, calls c.Next(), and flushes the writer; a miss with tsr set produces a 301 for GET (307 otherwise) via redirectTrailingSlash; the HandleMethodNotAllowed path scans the other method trees to build an Allow header; and everything else lands in serveError with the built-in 404 page not found body (Engine.handleHTTPRequest, L719).

Next, Abort, and the int8 Index Trick

The middleware chain is executed by one loop. Context.Next increments c.index and calls each pending handler in turn; because the loop condition is re-checked after every handler, a middleware that calls Next itself simply resumes the same loop afterward — nesting is an illusion created by the shared index (Context.Next, L197). That index is an int8, and the sentinel abortIndex is math.MaxInt8 >> 1, i.e. 63 (abortIndex, L57).

That explains two behaviors people find surprising. First, Abort only sets the index; the current handler continues to run — the doc comment says so explicitly — but nothing after it will fire, because no chain can legally reach 63 entries (Context.Abort, L216). Registration guards that invariant: combineHandlers asserts the merged chain stays below abortIndex and panics with “too many handlers” otherwise (RouterGroup.combineHandlers, L277). Second, AbortWithStatus writes the status code eagerly and then aborts, which is why auth middleware built on it returns 401 correctly (Context.AbortWithStatus, L222). Even Context.Copy sets the cloned index to abortIndex, so a Context handed to a goroutine can never re-enter the chain.

Bind and Validate: From Content-Type to Struct Tags

Binding is where Gin routes data into your structs, and the engine choice is explicit. Context.ShouldBind asks binding.Default to pick a strategy from the method and Content-Type (Context.ShouldBind, L860). The rule at binding.Default, L95 is blunt: any GET gets form binding, everything else switches on the MIME header across JSON, XML, ProtoBuf, MsgPack, YAML, TOML, BSON, and multipart. That is why ShouldBind on a GET with a JSON body reads the query string instead — call ShouldBindJSON explicitly if you mean the body.

The JSON path is a two-stage affair. jsonBinding.Bind hands the request body to decodeJSON, which uses Gin’s pluggable codec layer (sonic, go-json, jsoniter, or encoding/json) and then calls validate on the populated struct (decodeJSON, L44). validate delegates to the package-level Validator, which by default is a defaultValidator wrapping go-playground/validator v10, pinned at v10.30.3 in go.mod (binding.validate, L122). One gotcha lives in defaultValidator.lazyinit, L93: the validator is initialized with SetTagName("binding"), so your struct tags must read binding:"required" — a validate:"..." tag is silently inert.

The split between MustBindWith and ShouldBindWith matters too: the Bind* family auto-responds with 400 and aborts the chain on decode failure, while ShouldBind* returns the error and leaves the response to you (Context.MustBindWith, L832). It is the same output-oriented separation we liked in the FastAPI source tour, where validation errors also became part of the request contract rather than a side effect.

From Install to Your First Model

The quickstart is short enough to verify line-by-line in the README. Prerequisite: Go 1.26 or above (README, L47); the module itself declares go 1.26.0. Installation is one import — import "github.com/gin-gonic/gin" — and Go’s module system fetches it during the build (README, L52).

Your first “model” is the struct you bind. The canonical example (README, L62) creates the router with r := gin.Default() — which attaches Logger and Recovery middleware in one call (Engine.Default, L250) — registers r.GET("/ping", ...), responds with c.JSON(http.StatusOK, gin.H{"message": "pong"}), and serves with r.Run(). That last call wraps everything you now understand: it builds an http.Server whose handler is the Engine itself, with a default 10-second ReadHeaderTimeout to blunt slowloris attacks (Engine.Run, L566). Save it as main.go, run go run main.go, visit http://localhost:8080/ping, and you get the JSON pong. To make it a model, add type Ping struct with binding:"required" tags and call c.ShouldBindJSON — now the radix tree, the chain, and the validator are all working for you. The released version at the time of writing is v1.12.0 (Version, L8). If you prefer Python’s decorator style, the Flask source tour covers the same contract from the other side, and Node readers will find the routing vocabulary familiar from the Express source tour.

Honest Limits

  • The chain has a hard ceiling. Because the index is int8 and abortIndex is 63, a route plus its middleware can carry at most 62 handlers before registration panics (RouterGroup.combineHandlers, L277). Nobody hits this by accident, but code generators should know.
  • Route insertion is not safe under traffic. The doc comment on node.addRoute states “Not concurrency-safe!” in so many words (node.addRoute, L135) — register routes before serving, which is what the framework assumes.
  • Unknown JSON fields are ignored by default. EnableDecoderDisallowUnknownFields defaults to false, so a typo in your payload disappears silently until you flip the flag (EnableDecoderDisallowUnknownFields, L21).
  • The validator tag is binding, not validate, and the wrapper hard-codes that at init (defaultValidator.lazyinit, L93).
  • Escaped-path routing is opt-in and tricky: the engine docs mark UseRawPath as “only a hint” and defer to EscapedPath (Engine.UseRawPath, L144). The default net/url-decoded path is the safe lane.

None of these are bugs; they are design choices with visible seams, which is exactly why reading the source pays off. The same lesson — read the hot path, not the README — is what we found in the Go-built Caddy server, and it applies doubly to frameworks as small and sharp as Gin.
entry.summary: A source tour of gin-gonic/gin showing how one pooled Context, a per-method radix tree, and a single int8 index carry every request from ServeHTTP to your handler.

entry.title: Hono From the Inside: One fetch(), Three Routers, and the Onion That Runs on Every Runtime

link.title: Hono From the Inside: One fetch(), Three Routers, and the Onion That Runs on Every Runtime

entry.content:
You ship an API to Cloudflare Workers on Friday. Monday, a teammate wants the same service on a company VM running Node, and another team deploys it to Deno Deploy before lunch. On most stacks that means three bootstrap codebases, three server abstractions, and three places where the request path can quietly diverge. Hono takes the opposite bet: there is no server object, no createApplication, and no listen() anywhere in the framework. The entire framework is one Web-Standard function — Request in, Response out.

That single decision explains almost everything else you find in the tree. Every modern runtime already exposes fetch as its event contract, so Hono never has to own sockets, event loops, or HTTP parsing. Routing, middleware chaining, and response building are plain code that any runtime executes identically, and the runtime-specific work shrinks to a thin adapter whose only job is to translate a native event into a Request and hand it to the same entry point.

This post is a source tour of honojs/hono on the main branch. We follow one request through the actual tree: the abstract HonoBase class, the three routers behind the SmartRouter default, the koa-derived compose(), the lazily-built Context, and the adapter layer. Every symbol and line number below was verified against the actual repository — nothing here is paraphrased from documentation.

The request path at a glance: runtime adapters converge on app.fetch, dispatch consults exactly one router, and compose chains whatever matched.

Reading the overview from left to right:

  • Everything enters through one Web-Standard fetch defined on HonoBase, L114 — the class is deliberately abstract and its comment says it “does not have a router”; the concrete class injects one (fetch, L494).
  • The entry delegates to a private dispatch loop (#dispatch, L421) that first resolves the path with a runtime-overridable getPath, selected once in the constructor for strict or non-strict mode (L191, getPath, L106).
  • Route lookup is a single call on the Router contract — just add and match (Router, L29) — so the matching algorithm is a swappable strategy, not baked-in code (router.match, L434).
  • The default Hono constructor wires SmartRouter over two candidates: RegExpRouter first, TrieRouter as fallback (hono.ts, L28).
  • SmartRouter buffers route registrations, replays them into each candidate, and on the first real match permanently rebinds its own match to the winner (match, L21, L46).
  • A fresh Context is constructed per request with the path and match result pre-attached (L436) — nothing is parsed eagerly; param decoding happens only if a handler asks.
  • When exactly one handler matched, compose is skipped entirely and the handler is invoked directly — a deliberate hot-path optimization (L445).
  • Multi-handler matches go through compose, L15, whose recursive dispatch, L32 threads next() through the chain and records each handler’s position in req.routeIndex (L44).
  • The adapter layer is thin by design: the Lambda handle builds a Request, calls app.fetch, and serializes the result back (handle, L265, L294).

The detail view adds the single-handler fast path, SmartRouter's permanent rebind, the RegExpRouter matcher build, Context's lazy accessors, and compose's error routing.

Entry: one fetch, one dispatch loop

HonoBase is not a usable application on its own. The comment above its router field says it plainly: “This class is like an abstract class and does not have a router. To use it, inherit the class and implement router in the constructor” (hono-base.ts, L131). Route registration happens through generated methods and #addRoute (L401), which merges the base path, wraps the handler with route metadata, and pushes it into router.add. The use() registration for middleware routes under METHOD_NAME_ALL, the internal ALL constant (router.ts, L9).

On the request side, fetch forwards to #dispatch, which handles two subtleties before routing. First, HEAD requests are transparently re-dispatched as GET and wrapped in a null-body Response (L428). Second, the path is resolved through the strict-mode-aware getPath chosen at construction. After router.match and new Context, the branch: if only one handler matched, it is called directly with a synthesized next that falls back to the 404 handler; otherwise compose takes over (L465) and the result must leave the context finalized — otherwise dispatch throws the memorable error “Context is not finalized. Did you forget to return a Response object or await next()?” (L470).

Routers: three implementations, one smart default

The router contract is tiny: name, add(method, path, handler), match(method, path), plus a two-shape Result carrying handlers with parameter maps or a parameter stash (router.ts, L98). That contract is why the entire matching algorithm can change under your app without touching a handler.

RegExpRouter (L35) registers every path into per-method tries, and the first match triggers buildAllMatchers (L86), where each method’s routes are compiled into a single compressed matcher via trie.buildRegExp() (L104). One big regex plus a static map means no per-request loop — this is where the speed claim in the README comes from. The cost: once compiled, the matcher is frozen, and a late add throws MESSAGE_MATCHER_IS_ALREADY_BUILT (router.ts, L21). Paths the compiler cannot support raise UnsupportedPathError (router.ts, L103).

That error is exactly what SmartRouter exists to absorb. Its match replays the buffered routes into each candidate inside a try/catch; on UnsupportedPathError it moves to the next router (smart-router/router.ts, L40). The fallback, TrieRouter (L5), walks a recursive node tree and accepts any path syntax. The first successful match rebinds this.match to the winning router for the lifetime of the app and renames the composite — e.g. “SmartRouter + RegExpRouter” (L58). Bundle-budget apps can skip the machinery entirely: the tiny preset wires HonoBase straight to a linear PatternRouter (preset/tiny.ts, L11).

compose() and Context: the onion and its envelope

compose.ts is a 73-line descendant of koa-compose, and the docstring says so (compose.ts, L5). If you have read our Express source tour, the lineage will feel familiar — but note the differences: dispatch(i) runs middleware[i][0][0], passes () => dispatch(i + 1) as next, guards double-calls with “next() called multiple times” (L34), and — uniquely — writes the current index into context.req.routeIndex before every handler (L44). That one line is how c.req.param() later knows which matched route’s parameter map to read (request.ts, L99). Errors thrown as Error instances are diverted into context.error and the app’s onError (compose.ts, L53).

The built-in logger shows the onion shape in twelve lines: log the incoming request, await next(), log the outgoing status and elapsed time (middleware/logger/index.ts, L81). Python readers can map this directly onto ASGI middleware from our FastAPI source tour — the recursion differs, the layering is identical.

Context (context.ts, L293) is the envelope every layer passes around, and it is aggressively lazy. The constructor stores only the raw Request and options (L352); req builds a HonoRequest on first access (L366), and res creates a Response from prepared headers on first read (L403). The setter does real work: it merges headers from any earlier response — preserving set-cookie as multiple entries — and flips finalized to true (L414). Runtime-only accessors live here too: env bindings (L315) and executionCtx (L391), both throwing when the host runtime did not provide them.

The adapter layer: events become Requests

The README’s runtime list is long — Workers, Fastly Compute, Deno, Bun, Vercel, AWS Lambda, Lambda@Edge, Node.js (README, L21) — and the in-tree adapters show how little code each translation costs. The AWS Lambda adapter is the richest: handle (L265) picks a processor with getProcessor (L669) among four event shapes — API Gateway v2 (L436), API Gateway v1 (L478), ALB (L541), and Lambda@Edge-style Lattice (L625) — builds a Request, calls app.fetch (L294), then serializes the Response back into a Lambda result. The Vercel adapter is three lines that return app.fetch(req) (vercel/handler.ts, L7). Deno ships helper functions — serveStatic, toSSG, upgradeWebSocket, getConnInfo (deno/index.ts, L10) — rather than a server. And in module-worker style, the app object itself is the handler: export default app, exactly the snippet the package docstring leads with (index.ts, L7). Compare our Flask source tour: Flask binds to a WSGI server it configures; Hono binds to nothing and is embeddable anywhere a Request type exists.

From Install to Your First Model

Hono’s quickstart is one command from the README: npm create hono@latest (README, L37), which scaffolds a project for your chosen runtime and template. The smallest possible app needs no scaffold at all — the README’s intro snippet (L25) is complete and runnable on any runtime that speaks fetch:

import { Hono } from 'hono'
const app = new Hono()

app.get('/', (c) => c.text('Hono!'))

export default app

The two facts to notice: the Hono import resolves to the class that installs SmartRouter by default (hono.ts, L28), and the app object is returned directly — there is no app.listen because the host runtime calls app.fetch for you. From there, handlers like c.text and c.json (context.ts, L700, L726) build responses through the same lazy Context we traced above, so your first JSON endpoint — for instance, an inference status route backed by a model service — exercises precisely the dispatch, router, and compose code path diagrammed here. Zero runtime dependencies and the Web-Standard API mean the identical file runs on Workers, Deno, and Bun; the README’s tiny preset claim of under 12kB (L43) covers deployments where every byte of cold start matters.

Honest Limits

  • There is no Node.js adapter in this tree. src/adapter contains aws-lambda, bun, cloudflare-workers, cloudflare-pages, deno, lambda-edge, netlify, service-worker, and vercel — Node support (README L21, L44) is delivered by ecosystem packages outside this repository, so Node-specific behavior cannot be verified from this clone.
  • Adapter code is mid-migration out of the core package. The Deno adapter docstring says it “will be removed from the hono package in v5” in favor of @hono/deno (deno/index.ts, L5); the Vercel (L5) and Bun (server.ts, L12) adapters carry the same deprecation notes.
  • Routing freezes at first request. Once SmartRouter selects a winner it drops its route buffer (smart-router/router.ts, L47), and any later add throws MESSAGE_MATCHER_IS_ALREADY_BUILT. Dynamic route registration after the first match is not possible.
  • compose routes only Error instances into onError (compose.ts, L53); anything else propagates, and #handleError rethrows non-Errors too (hono-base.ts, L414). Throwing strings bypasses your error handler.
  • HEAD is emulated by re-dispatching as GET and discarding the body (hono-base.ts, L428), so handlers run twice the work of a bare 404 even though the client sees no body.
  • RegExpRouter’s one-matcher-for-all-routes design is fast but all-or-nothing: unsupported path syntax forces SmartRouter onto the slower tree walk for the entire app, not just the offending route.
entry.summary: A verified source tour of honojs/hono showing how a single Web-Standard fetch entry point, a self-optimizing router trio, koa-style compose, a lazy Context, and thin runtime adapters carry one request from event to Response.

entry.title: Phoenix From the Inside: How One Request Becomes Compiled Code

link.title: Phoenix From the Inside: How One Request Becomes Compiled Code

entry.content:
Every few months a benchmark resurfaces where Elixir’s Phoenix holds millions of concurrent WebSocket connections on a single box while ordinary HTTP responses still return in microseconds, and every time the same skepticism follows: developers raised on thread-per-request cannot see where the request threads are. The honest answer is that there are none, and that the secret is not only the BEAM virtual machine. Phoenix itself is architected so that almost nothing on the hot path is interpreted at request time. The parts of the framework that other projects treat as runtime tables or loop-driven dispatchers are, in Phoenix, artifacts the compiler emits when you build your application.

The clearest proof is routing. Most web frameworks walk a list of regexes or trie nodes per request. Phoenix compiles every route into pattern-match function clauses when your app compiles; at request time the router calls a generated function and the VM solves the match in one pass. The same holds for the endpoint, whose plug chain is generated code with error wrapping baked in, for the pipe groups that run before your controller, and for the realtime layer, where each joined channel topic is a supervised process with its own mailbox.

This post is a source tour of phoenixframework/phoenix, checked out on the main branch at commit 79fdbb5ed552. It follows one coherent HTTP request from the adapter process to the controller, then takes an aside into channels. Every symbol, file and line number cited below was verified against the actual tree with grep — nothing here is from memory or from documentation.

Overview: how the endpoint supervision tree boots, how an HTTP request flows through the generated plug chain and compiled route clauses, and how socket paths fork into the channel world.

Reading the overview from left to right:

  • Boot is a tree, not a server. Phoenix.Endpoint.Supervisor.init/1, L28 assembles one :one_for_one supervisor from configuration, warmup, PubSub, socket and server children at L101. The HTTP server itself is just another child: server_children/3, L187 asks the configured adapter for child specs.
  • Request entry is generated. Endpoint call/2, L668 stamps script_name, secret_key_base and the :phoenix_endpoint private key, then invokes the app’s chain. The override and its rescue/catch funnel everything into RenderErrors.__catch__/5, L54, so error rendering cannot be forgotten by a plug.
  • Sockets get first crack. socket_dispatch/2, L703 is the first plug in the chain and pattern-matches the path against every declared socket; unmatched paths fall through to the plugs you declared, ending at the router.
  • The router is a case expression. Router call/2, L467 URI-decodes each path segment and runs case __match_route__(method, decoded, host); the clauses come from build_match_path/5, L748, and a miss hits the catch-all at L605 that raises NoRouteError.
  • Match results carry code, not data. A clause returns a tuple containing a pre-compiled pipe-chain function and the target plug; the shared Route.prepare/3, L192 merges params, private and assigns, a comment there noting that sharing one clause makes large routers compile faster.
  • Dispatch is instrumented. Router __call__/5, L412 emits :phoenix, :router_dispatch telemetry at L417, runs the compiled pipe function, then calls plug.call/2, L428 inside a try/rescue that still reports telemetry on exceptions.
  • The realtime fork is ordinary Plug. Transports.WebSocket.call/2, L39 runs code reload, logging and origin checks, then WebSockAdapter.upgrade/4, L79 turns the HTTP conn into a long-lived socket; joins spawn channel processes through Channel.Server.join/4, L19.
  • Development mode is a plug too. The generated endpoint declares Phoenix.CodeReloader before the router, whose call/2, L112 invokes the configured reloader on every request and renders a compile-error page instead of the response on failure; socket transports rerun the same reload via Socket.Transport.code_reload/3, L310 before upgrading.

Detail: the same request path with every generated artifact made explicit — `__before_compile__` overrides, route clause builders, deduplicated pipe groups, the code reloader and per-channel GenServers under a partitioned pool supervisor.

The Endpoint Is Code the Compiler Wrote for You

use Phoenix.Endpoint does three things worth reading closely. First, it makes your endpoint a Plug.Builder, so the plug chain you declare is compiled once into nested function calls. Second, it wires plug :socket_dispatch ahead of your own plugs at L513, generated per socket by __before_compile__ at L651. Third, it overrides call/2 itself, so the very first thing every request does is set the endpoint’s identity and get wrapped in error handling.

Configuration reads are also compile-friendly. The generated config/2 does an :ets.lookup on the endpoint’s own table, L549, and boot warms URL and static-manifest data into :persistent_term at L363 — so per-request lookups avoid ETS contention entirely. Compared with the runtime option-matching you find in the Flask source tour, the difference is philosophical: Phoenix pays everything at compile time.

The error wrapping is not decorative. Because the override wraps the whole chain, a plug that raises anywhere below the endpoint — a parser blowing up on malformed JSON, a controller crashing mid-render — is caught by the same two clauses and rerendered through RenderErrors, which is also what powers the debug banner in dev. The router adds a second, narrower layer of the same pattern around the final plug call, so dispatch telemetry still records the exception before it propagates.

Route Matching Is Pattern Matching, Not a Loop

Phoenix.Router.__before_compile__ at L499 takes the routes your get, post and match macros accumulated and asks Route.exprs/1, L121 to turn each into a path match, a bindings list and a dispatch tuple. build_match_path/5 then emits one function clause per route, and pipe groups are deduplicated into shared __pipe_throughN__ functions at L774 so ten routes using :browser compile one chain. The pipe-group macro itself compiles your plugs via Plug.Builder.compile at L964 — the same machinery the plug macro accumulates at L996.

Setting group_by :verb switches the shape entirely: dispatch clauses are grouped into __match_route_GET__-style helpers (L707) so a request only scans routes for its method. This is the design payoff over a dynamic route table like the one in the Express source tour — the VM’s clause selection is doing what a hand-written trie does elsewhere, and the Actix Web source tour reaches a similar place only through macro-generated match arms.

The compiler also generates validation you get for free. __before_compile__ emits a __checks__ block that references every plug’s init function (L538), so a typo’d plug module fails at compile time rather than on the first request. A separate __verify_route__ lookup backs path helpers, letting generated URL helpers catch bad paths early instead of guessing at runtime.

Channels: One Process Per Conversation, Under Supervision

Channels are where the supervision tree earns its keep. At boot, socket_children/3, L139 starts every socket declared with the socket macro; each socket’s child_spec starts a Phoenix.Socket.PoolSupervisor, L467 whose init/1, L47 creates partitioned supervisors and registers an ETS ref via Phoenix.Config.permanent. A join therefore costs one GenServer out of a pool, not one out of a global registry.

Message flow stays symmetric. Server.join/4, L19 runs your join/3 callback and links the transport; incoming events arrive as handle_info and dispatch to your handle_in/3 at L335. Replies use Channel.reply/2, L686, one-to-one pushes bypass PubSub via push/3, L640, and broadcasts go through broadcast/3, L571 to Server.broadcast/4, L148 and Phoenix.PubSub. The intercept macro, L534 lets you filter outgoing events per topic. Topic-to-channel routing is itself compiled pattern matching, courtesy of the channel macro at L401 — "room:*" is a clause, not a string scan.

Shutdown is supervised as well. Alongside the pool, socket_children/3 starts drainer specs, and Phoenix.Socket.PoolDrainer, L66 is a trap-exit GenServer whose terminate/2 collects the channel processes from every partition supervisor and sends each one a phx_drain broadcast in rounds of ten thousand with a two-second pause between rounds by default, emitting [:phoenix, :socket_drain] telemetry as it goes. That is how graceful deploys of long-lived connections are handled, and it is implemented in roughly a hundred lines rather than a framework-within-a-framework.

From Install to Your First Model

The README keeps installation short: follow the official installation guide, or run the source installer directly from the clone — cd phoenix/installer then mix phx.new dev_app --dev (L37), which wires your app to the local Phoenix checkout as a path dependency. Building the framework itself is just mix deps.get and mix compile (L59).

Your first “model” in Phoenix terms is the generated endpoint module, and the installer template shows the shape every request will take: Plug.RequestId, Plug.Telemetry, Plug.Parsers, Plug.MethodOverride, Plug.Head, Plug.Session, then your router. A /live socket with websocket and longpoll transports is declared a few lines above, though the generated socket dispatch only wires longpoll handlers when you opt in — the endpoint reads Keyword.get(:longpoll, false) at L742. Defaults matter: the websocket transport ships with a 60-second timeout and compression off (L26). Reading that file end to end teaches more about Phoenix than any tutorial, because it is the literal list of plugs your production traffic will traverse.

Honest Limits

Everything above is verified, but so are the trade-offs. The default adapter is still Cowboy2Adapter with a code comment deferring the Bandit default to 2.0, even though generated apps already prefer Bandit. The :pubsub key on an endpoint is deprecated in favor of starting PubSub in your application tree (L117), and the endpoint init/2 callback is deprecated too. The code reloader is disabled by default (code_reloader: false in the defaults at L235) and only drives the compilers listed in :reloadable_compilers.

Two structural limits follow from the design. Routes are frozen at compile time because they exist as function clauses — adding one means recompiling, which is why dev-mode CodeReloader.call/2, L112 exists at all. And channel state lives in per-process memory: when the transport goes away, the DOWN handling at L363 stops the channel, and any state it held must be rebuilt or persisted elsewhere.
entry.summary: A source tour of phoenixframework/phoenix on main showing how the Endpoint, compiled route clauses, Plug dispatch, channel supervision and code reloading turn every request into compiler-generated code.

entry.title: Agno Under the Hood: A Source Tour of the Full-Stack Agent Runtime

link.title: Agno Under the Hood: A Source Tour of the Full-Stack Agent Runtime

entry.content:
Ask any team what it takes to ship one production agent, and the answer is usually a shopping list: a model client for your provider, a vector database for document retrieval, a memory store for user facts, somewhere durable to persist sessions, and a hand-rolled loop that stitches tool calls together. That is five repositories, five sets of dependency versions, and five distinct places for things to break at 2 a.m. Composable stacks like LangChain give you excellent parts, but the seams between the parts remain yours to hold together.

Agno takes the opposite bet: the runtime ships the whole stack. A single Agent object carries tools, a knowledge base, memory, and storage hooks; Team coordinates several agents; Workflow chains steps deterministically. Everything lives in one package under libs/agno/agno/ in the monorepo, distributed as the agno package (pyproject.toml, L2, currently version 3.1.12). As the finale of our agent-framework source tours, it is the batteries-included runtime that stops asking you to glue libraries together.

This tour pins the code at main and asks one question: what actually happens between agent.run("...") and the returned text? We follow Agent.run, L1523 through system-prompt assembly, knowledge and memory retrieval, the provider tool loop, and the final structured response — then map where Team, L83 orchestration and session persistence plug in. The two diagrams below render the same tour at different zoom levels.

Agno overview: one Agent.run fans out into context assembly, the model/tool loop, and persistence; Team and Workflow wrap the very same runtime rather than replacing it.

Reading the overview from left to right:

  • Agent.run is a dispatcher. The public run, L1523 signature resolves to _run.run_dispatch (agent.py, L1549); the real work lives in numbered stages inside _run, L367 and its async twin _arun, L1513.
  • The system prompt is assembled, not templated. get_run_messages, L1921 calls get_system_message, L959, which concatenates the description, <your_role>, <instructions>, and <additional_information> blocks (_messages.py, L1092) — adding current time and even approximate location when enabled.
  • Knowledge rides two paths. The prompt gets a proactive build_context injection (_messages.py, L1208); agentic RAG instead exposes a search_knowledge_base, L5489 tool whose Knowledge.search, L1187 queries the vector store and rescores results with a reranker (knowledge.py, L1248).
  • Memory extraction runs in the background. astart_memory_task, L139 launches it concurrently with generation (_run.py, L2305); recall goes through search_user_memories, L603 on MemoryManager, L46.
  • The tool loop belongs to the Model, not the Agent. Model.response, L651 runs a while True loop (base.py, L705) that re-calls the provider until tool calls are exhausted, honoring tool_call_limit (base.py, L657).
  • Toolkits compile to Functions. Toolkit.register, L273 wraps plain callables into Function, L1215 schemas; FunctionCall.execute, L2598 runs the entrypoint, and confirmation gates are checked back in the model loop (base.py, L852).
  • Structured output is post-processing. With response_model set, get_response_format, L857 hands the provider a JSON schema and convert_response_to_structured_format, L904 parses the final text into your Pydantic model inside RunOutput, L650.
  • One save path for every component. save_session, L231 persists AgentSession, TeamSession, and WorkflowSession alike; BaseDb.upsert_session, L683 is the single write every backend implements.
  • Teams coordinate by tool call. In the default coordinate mode (_init.py, L231), a leader agent delegates through delegate_task_to_member, L713, governed by TeamMode, L6.

Agno detail: the numbered stages of Agent._arun, the provider tool loop inside Model.response, team delegation, and the single session-upsert path.

One Runtime, Five Primitives

The monorepo layout tells the design story. agent/ holds the Agent class (agent.py, L82) plus nine private modules — _run.py, _messages.py, _response.py, _tools.py, _session.py — that split the runtime into testable units. Open _arun, L1513 and the stages are literally numbered in comments: tools resolve first via determine_tools_for_model, L2260, messages assemble at stage 6, memory extraction starts at stage 7, reasoning runs at stage 8, and the model answers at stage 9. There is also a resume path: continue_run, L1685 and its async twin acontinue_run, L1769 replay a stored checkpoint, which is how a paused run — say, one waiting on a tool confirmation — picks up without losing state. team/ and workflow/ reuse the same session and message machinery rather than reimplementing it, which is why a Workflow step can embed a Team that embeds Agents without any adapter code. Tools are a registry concern: add_tool, L853 accepts a Toolkit, a callable, or a raw dict and normalizes everything into Function objects. Knowledge (Knowledge, L86) and memory are injected as components, so swapping PgVector, L65 for Qdrant or Milvus changes one constructor argument, not the run loop. Workflows compose the other primitives declaratively: Workflow, L643 takes steps built from Step, Loop, Parallel, Router, and Condition operators, each with its own module under workflow/, so deterministic stages and agent decisions mix in one graph. And when a provider call dies mid-run, _try_fallback_models, L387 retries the prompt on the next entry in fallback_models, emitting a fallback_model_activated event so clients know the answer came from plan B.

From Install to Your First Model

The README has pivoted to a coding-agent-first flow: it suggests handing your coding agent a prompt that clones the agentos-railway template and follows a setup skill (README.md, L33), with prebuilt templates for Docker, Railway, AWS, GCP, and more (README.md, L56). If you just want the library, the distribution is named agno (pyproject.toml, L2), so pip install agno or uv add agno is enough; contributors instead clone the repo and run pip install uv plus ./scripts/dev_setup.sh (CONTRIBUTING.md, L39). The first agent from cookbook/02_agents/01_quickstart/basic_agent.py is deliberately minimal:

from agno.agent import Agent
from agno.models.openai import OpenAIResponses

agent = Agent(
    name="Quickstart Agent",
    model=OpenAIResponses(id="gpt-5.2"),
)

agent.print_response("Say hello and introduce yourself in one sentence.", stream=True)

Every model provider lives behind the same Model, L134 interface — invoke, L553 is the single provider call — so switching from OpenAI to Anthropic is an import change.

Inside the Tool Loop

The async run reaches the model in stage 9: _arun, L2338 hands control to ahandle_model_response_stream, L1193, which wraps the provider call in acall_model_stream_with_fallback, L328 — a wrapper that detects context-overflow errors, compacts history, and can activate fallback models. Tool calls stream back as events, get dispatched by handle_tool_call_updates, L1086, and execute through run_tool, L869 after determine_tools_for_model, L662 has resolved which toolkits the chosen provider supports. Stage 8, just before the model call, belongs to reasoning: ahandle_reasoning_stream, L125 gives the model a scratchpad pass and emits step-by-step events. Structured output can then take one of two extra passes — a cheap parser model rewriting the first answer (parse_response_with_parser_model, L349) or a dedicated output model finishing the run (generate_response_with_output_model, L582). Everything surfaces as typed events on the result object — ToolCallStartedEvent, L427, SessionSummaryStartedEvent, L388 — so a UI can render exactly what the runtime is doing. Where LangGraph internals make the loop an explicit state machine you compile yourself, Agno hides the loop inside Model.response and exposes controls — limits, confirmation gates, streaming events — at the edges.

Teams: Coordination as a Tool Call

Team.run, L917 delegates to its own dispatch module (_run.py, L1902) and branches on TeamMode, L6: coordinate has a leader model pick members and craft tasks; route sends work to one specialist and returns its answer untouched; broadcast gives the same task to every member, concurrently under arun. The modes compile into two flags at construction: route sets respond_directly, broadcast sets delegate_to_all_members, and anything else falls back to coordinate (_init.py, L216). A fourth mode, tasks, decomposes a goal into a shared task list and loops until the work is done. The clever part is that coordination is implemented as ordinary tool calls — the leader receives delegate_task_to_member, L713 like any other function, so no separate planner process exists. Members can be Agents or whole Teams (team.py, L88), which is how hierarchies form. If you liked CrewAI’s role-play framing, Teams feel similar, but the member-selection logic here is just the same tool loop you read above, running one level up.

Where State Lives

Three stores cover state. Sessions: get_session, L574 and upsert_session, L683 on BaseDb, L302, with sixteen adapters from Postgres and SQLite to Mongo, Dynamo, and Firestore. Memory: MemoryManager, L46 extracts per-user facts with a model call and reads them back via search_user_memories, emitting MemoryUpdateStartedEvent, L377 when the background task fires. Knowledge: documents flow into one of twenty-one vector-store adapters, each implementing the same search contract, and tenancy is handled inside the query — Knowledge.search, L1187 forwards a user_id scope to the store (knowledge.py, L1246) and injects an instance-scope filter (knowledge.py, L1230). That memory layer is the main overlap with Mem0 — which does exactly this one thing, with deeper graph variants — while Agno trades that depth for keeping memory, RAG, and sessions on one config object.

Honest Limits

  • Telemetry is on by default. Agno sends one event per agent; disable it with AGNO_TELEMETRY=false (README.md, L96). No prompts or outputs are transmitted, but it is worth knowing on day one.
  • The README no longer contains a quickstart. Setup flows through docs.agno.com links and cloud templates, so the repo front door assumes you want the AgentOS platform, not just the runtime library (README.md, L17).
  • Version churn is real. The package sits at 3.1.12 with a platform pivot behind it; code written against older releases needs migration review before upgrading.
  • Config sharp edges exist. Setting a reranker on both Knowledge and the vector db raises a warning because only one component may own rescoring (knowledge.py, L172).
  • Breadth over depth. Twenty-one vector stores and sixteen session stores is impressive surface, but each adapter inherits the store’s quirks; budget time to validate the one you actually deploy. Python support is >=3.9,<4 (pyproject.toml, L5).
entry.summary: A guided source tour of Agno: how Agent.run assembles the system prompt, runs the tool loop, persists sessions, and where Teams and Workflows coordinate members.

entry.title: AutoGen Under the Hood: A Source Tour of Microsoft’s Multi-Agent Runtime

link.title: AutoGen Under the Hood: A Source Tour of Microsoft’s Multi-Agent Runtime

entry.content:
One agent with one while-loop is fine until the day your task needs a researcher, a coder, and a critic at the same time. Then you either cram all three personalities into one context window and hope, or you hand-roll threading code that breaks the first time an agent’s output has to become another agent’s input. The wall you hit is orchestration: who speaks next, who answers whom, when the whole thing has produced enough debate, and how to recover when one participant goes off the rails. A bare agent loop has no answer for any of that.

AutoGen, Microsoft’s open-source multi-agent framework, rebuilt itself in v0.4 around exactly this wall. Instead of shipping agent “recipes”, it ships primitives: agents are actors, a runtime routes every message, teams are group chats moderated by a dedicated manager agent, and stopping is a composable condition object rather than a hardcoded limit. Where LangChain composes steps into a graph and LlamaIndex leans data-first, AutoGen’s bet is that orchestration is fundamentally a message-passing problem — the same bet actor systems have made for decades.

This tour walks the source of autogen-core and autogen-agentchat to show how that bet pays off: an asyncio envelope queue, topic-based publish/subscribe, RPC futures, a group chat protocol with four selectable speaker policies, and a tool loop with reflection. By the end you’ll see how an event-driven runtime turns N chatting agents into a real orchestration engine.

AutoGen at a glance: AgentChat teams (top) register participants and a manager on the core runtime; every turn is routed as a message envelope; agents reply through model clients and tools until a termination condition fires and a TaskResult comes back.

Reading the overview from left to right:

  • The team is a driver, not a scheduler. run_stream, L351 starts an embedded runtime, registers participants plus a manager, and sends one GroupChatStart — the rest of the run is pure message flow.
  • One queue to route them all. SingleThreadedAgentRuntime, L149 keeps every RPC, publish and response as an envelope in a single asyncio queue (_message_queue, L257).
  • Two verbs, two semantics. send_message, L332 is point-to-point RPC returning a future; publish_message, L387 is fire-and-forget onto a topic.
  • Fan-out is subscription-based. _process_publish, L557 resolves subscribers for the topic, skips the sender, and asyncio.gathers delivery to all of them.
  • Subscriptions bind topics to agents. TypeSubscription, L10 maps a topic type onto an agent type; map_to_agent, L56 derives the exact AgentId from the topic’s source key.
  • Each chat agent wears an actor shell. ChatAgentContainer, L24 buffers the shared thread and, on handle_request, L86, calls the wrapped agent’s on_messages_stream.
  • The agent itself is model plumbing. AssistantAgent, L90 builds context and streams through the provider-agnostic ChatCompletionClient, L209 contract.
  • Memory plugs into the agent, not the runtime. update_context, L78 lets any Memory, L60 store inject retrieved content into the model context before a call.
  • Stopping is explicit. The manager applies a TerminationCondition, L15 after every turn; MaxMessageTermination, L62 is the simplest of a dozen composable stops.

The detail view: envelope dispatch and intervention on the left, the GroupChatStart → request → response protocol in the middle, four speaker-selection policies above, and AssistantAgent's tool loop with providers and tools below.

The Runtime Is a Message Bus with Actors

The core abstraction is the AgentRuntime, L21 protocol: send_message, publish_message, register_factory. Agents never call each other; they only address the runtime, which is what makes orchestration swappable — the in-process SingleThreadedAgentRuntime, L149 and a gRPC worker runtime in autogen-ext implement the same surface.

Dispatch is a pattern match. Both entry verbs stay thin — send_message and publish_message validate, serialize, and enqueue their envelope, then return immediately — while a host task started by start() drains the queue until stop_when_idle, L844 observes it empty, which is exactly how teams end a run. _process_next, L671 pulls one envelope and inspects its type: RPC envelopes go to _process_send, L466, publishes to _process_publish, L557, and responses to _process_response, L632, which finally resolves the future that send_message handed back to the original caller. Before any delivery, registered InterventionHandler, L20 hooks may rewrite or drop the message — a clean audit and guard rail seam.

Agents come in three flavors. BaseAgent, L60 is the abstract actor with a classmethod register that wraps a lazy factory (register_factory, L886, invoked on first contact by _invoke_agent_factory, L942). RoutedAgent, L415 adds decorator-dispatched message handlers, and ClosureAgent, L76 turns a bare async function into an agent. Every delivery carries a MessageContext, L9 with sender, topic, and the is_rpc flag that separates request/response from event flow.

Group Chats Are a Manager Agent Plus a Protocol

AgentChat is “just” a protocol on top of that bus. BaseGroupChat, L40 wires each participant as a ChatAgentContainer and adds one more actor: the manager (_init, L191). Wiring is all subscriptions — each participant listens on its own topic and the shared group topic, while the manager also subscribes to the output topic so streamed events reach your console.

The turn cycle is three messages. GroupChatStart, L38 reaches the manager’s handle_start; the manager decides who speaks and publishes GroupChatRequestPublish, L68; the named container runs its agent and broadcasts a GroupChatAgentResponse, L48, which lands in handle_agent_response, L135. There the manager applies the termination check (_apply_termination_condition, L195) and, if the chat lives on, _transition_to_next_speakers, L172 requests the next speaker. On the consumer side, run_stream loops on an output queue, yielding messages until a GroupChatTermination event carries the stop reason — and the caller’s cancellation token is linked to the pending receive, so a hung stream can still be killed. When the stop condition fires, the team’s stream ends via stop_when_idle and yields a TaskResult. Where LangGraph models this loop as an explicit state machine you draw (we toured that in the LangGraph internals walkthrough), AutoGen hides the edges inside a conversation protocol and a policy method.

Four Ways to Pick the Next Speaker

Every policy is the same manager base class with a different select_speaker. RoundRobinGroupChatManager, L16 just increments a cyclic index — deterministic and free. SelectorGroupChatManager, L50 asks an LLM: its select_speaker, L152 honors an optional custom selector function first, builds a roles-plus-transcript prompt, then _select_speaker, L232 retries JSON votes and falls back to mention counts (_mentioned_agents, L310).

The other two policies are conversational. The Swarm manager (SwarmGroupChatManager, L15) scans the thread backwards for the latest HandoffMessage and follows it — handoffs themselves are tool calls generated from the declarative Handoff, L12 spec via handoff_tool. And MagenticOneOrchestrator, L58 — the Magentic-One pattern — maintains a task ledger plus a JSON progress ledger: _orchestrate_step, L300 detects stalls, re-plans or redirects, and eventually _prepare_final_answer, L478 asks a designated agent to produce the answer.

Inside AssistantAgent’s Tool Loop

AssistantAgent, L90 is where the rubber meets the model. Before each call it refreshes context — including _update_model_context_with_memory, L1028, which invokes the pluggable Memory, L60 protocol so a vector-store-backed store (say, Qdrant behind your own corpus) can inject retrieved facts. If your retrieval needs outgrow agent-adjacent memory and become the product itself, that’s a data framework’s job — see our LlamaIndex source tour.

Then create or create_stream runs, and _process_model_result, L1118 loops up to max_tool_iterations: yield a ToolCallRequestEvent, execute every FunctionCall concurrently through BaseTool, L96 or a Workbench, L78 (the MCP-style tool service), emit results, and either reflect on tool use with a final LLM call (_reflect_on_tool_use_flow, L1409) or summarize. The loop is bounded, which is precisely the recovery knob a bare while-loop lacks. Streaming survives all of it: with model_client_stream=True, token chunks arrive as ModelClientStreamingChunkEvent, L529 in the same event stream your UI consumes, and tool execution results stream through an internal queue so progress is never buffered until the end.

From Install to Your First Model

The README keeps it to two packages: Python 3.10+ and pip install -U "autogen-agentchat" "autogen-ext[openai]" (Installation, L38). AgentChat is the high-level API; autogen-ext carries the provider clients (OpenAI, Azure, Anthropic, Ollama) plus extras like caching. Export OPENAI_API_KEY and the Hello World is eight lines (Quickstart, L53):

import asyncio
from autogen_agentchat.agents import AssistantAgent
from autogen_ext.models.openai import OpenAIChatCompletionClient

async def main() -> None:
    model_client = OpenAIChatCompletionClient(model="gpt-4.1")
    agent = AssistantAgent("assistant", model_client=model_client)
    print(await agent.run(task="Say 'Hello World!'"))
    await model_client.close()

asyncio.run(main())

Swap the agent for a RoundRobinGroupChat([agent1, agent2], termination_condition=MaxMessageTermination(10)) and you have a team; .run() returns a TaskResult with every message and the stop reason. For a no-code UI there’s AutoGen Studio (pip install -U autogenstudio).

Honest Limits

The same conversation-centric design sets the ceilings. First, every turn is a full LLM round-trip per agent, and long threads make every subsequent call bigger — group chats with LLM-based selection pay an extra selection call on top. The mitigations are explicit: token- and message-aware stops like TokenUsageTermination, L235, sentinel phrases via TextMentionTermination, L111, ExternalTermination, L404 for human-in-the-loop stops, and bounded model context via ChatCompletionContext, L10. Nothing structural stops a team from politely agreeing with itself, though — if you want hard guarantees about who runs when, a drawn graph gives you edges a conversation cannot.

Second, the runtime you get by default is single-process asyncio; scaling past one box means the gRPC worker runtime from autogen-ext, which is real distributed-systems work (message ordering, host availability) that AutoGen doesn’t hide from you. Third, v0.4 is a deliberate break: the README points v0.2 users at a migration guide (Releases, L41), and code from the old pyautogen API does not carry over. None of these are disqualifiers — they’re the cost of a framework that puts the orchestration seam in the open instead of burying it in an agent loop.
entry.summary: A source-level tour of microsoft/autogen: how SingleThreadedAgentRuntime routes message envelopes, how group chat managers pick the next speaker, and how AssistantAgent runs its tool-call loop.
